question.prompt: For integers \(k\) and \(n\) such that \(1\le k\lt n,\) let \[ \binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}. \] Then \(\left(\frac{n-2k-1}{k+1}\right)\binom nk\) is an integer

solutions.explanation:
The denominator \(k+1\) suggests comparing \(\binom nk\) with \(\binom n{k+1}\). From the factorial formula,
\[
\frac{n-k}{k+1}\binom nk
=\frac{n!}{(k+1)!(n-k-1)!}
=\binom n{k+1}.
\]
These factorials are defined because \(1\le k<n\), so \(k+1\le n\) and \(n-k-1\ge0\). Also, \(k+1>0\), so no division by zero occurs.

Now split the given numerator as
\[
n-2k-1=(n-k)-(k+1).
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{n-2k-1}{k+1}\binom nk
&=\left(\frac{n-k}{k+1}-1\right)\binom nk\\
&=\binom n{k+1}-\binom nk.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each binomial coefficient is an integer because it counts selections of the indicated size from \(n\) distinct objects. Both selection sizes are allowed here, including the endpoint \(k=n-1\), when \(\binom n{k+1}=\binom nn=1\). Their difference is therefore always an integer. The answer is \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
solutions.title: Recognize a difference of binomial coefficients
